pages.subtitle: A quiet sister in Paris who saw Mary and was asked to make the Miraculous Medal.

quick_facts.label: Known for
quick_facts.value: The Miraculous Medal and her quiet, humble service

pages.intro: Catherine Labouré grew up on a farm in France. When she was a young sister with the Daughters of Charity in Paris, Mary appeared to her and asked her to have a medal made. Millions of people now wear the Miraculous Medal. But Catherine spent the rest of her life quietly caring for elderly people, and almost no one knew her secret.
story_paragraphs: Catherine was born on May 2, 1806, in France. She was the ninth of eleven children. When she was nine years old, her mother died. Catherine picked up a statue of Mary, held it close, and said, "Now you will be my mother."

As she grew up, Catherine took care of her family's home. She wanted to give her life to God. In 1830, she joined the Daughters of Charity, sisters who serve the poor, at their house on the Rue du Bac in Paris.

On the night of July 18, 1830, a child woke Catherine and led her to the chapel. There she saw Mary, seated in a chair. Catherine knelt and rested her hands on Mary's lap. Mary told her that graces would be given to all who ask with confidence at the foot of the altar.

On November 27, 1830, Mary appeared to Catherine again, during evening prayer. Mary stood with rays of light shining from her hands. Around her were the words, "O Mary, conceived without sin, pray for us who have recourse to thee." Mary asked Catherine to have a medal made with this picture. On the back would be a cross, the letter M, and two hearts, for Jesus and Mary.
Catherine told only her priest. After about two years, the archbishop allowed the medals to be made. So many people received graces through it that it came to be called the Miraculous Medal.

Catherine never told anyone else that she was the sister who had seen Mary. For about 46 years, she quietly cared for elderly people near Paris. She died on December 31, 1876. Only then did people learn her secret.

pages.subtitle: A young priest from Bohemia who crossed the ocean and became a bishop who built Catholic schools in America.

quick_facts.label: From
quick_facts.value: Bohemia (now the Czech Republic); served in the United States

quick_facts.label: Known for
quick_facts.value: Building Catholic schools and caring for immigrant families

pages.intro: John Neumann was born in Bohemia, in what is now the Czech Republic. He wanted to be a priest in America, so he crossed the ocean when he was 25. He traveled long distances to serve families who had moved to America from other countries. As bishop of Philadelphia, he built a whole system of Catholic schools.
story_paragraphs: John Neumann was born on March 28, 1811, in a small town in Bohemia. He was a bright student and studied in the city of Prague. He wanted to become a priest and serve as a missionary.

In Bohemia, there were already plenty of priests. But in America, many Catholic families had no priest at all. So when he was 25, John crossed the Atlantic Ocean to New York. Soon after he arrived, he was ordained a priest.

Father Neumann served German-speaking immigrant families in New York, Maryland, Virginia and Ohio. Many of them were poor farmers and workers living far apart. He walked and rode long distances to reach them, to celebrate Mass, and to teach the children.
When he was 29, he joined the Redemptorists, a community of priests who preach to people in need. He was the first Redemptorist to make his vows in the United States.

In 1852, when he was 41, John was made bishop of Philadelphia. He was a small man and very humble, but he worked very hard. He organized the parish schools of Philadelphia into one system, so that more children could go to Catholic school. In a short time, the number of students grew almost twenty times.
On January 5, 1860, Bishop Neumann died suddenly in Philadelphia. He was only 48 years old. People remembered him as a holy, hardworking shepherd who loved children and families.
In 1977, Pope Paul VI declared John Neumann a saint. He was the first man who was a citizen of the United States to be named a saint. He is buried in Philadelphia.

pages.subtitle: A French sister who opened the first free school west of the Mississippi, and whom the Potawatomi called "Woman-Who-Prays-Always."

quick_facts.label: From
quick_facts.value: Grenoble, France; served in Missouri and Kansas

quick_facts.label: Known for
quick_facts.value: Her schools on the American frontier and her life of prayer

pages.intro: Rose Philippine Duchesne grew up in France and dreamed of being a missionary. When she was 49, she finally sailed to America. In a log cabin in St. Charles, Missouri, she opened the first free school west of the Mississippi River. When she was 72, she went to live among the Potawatomi people, who gave her a beautiful name.
story_paragraphs: Philippine Duchesne was born on August 29, 1769, in Grenoble, France. Her father taught her about public life, and her mother taught her to love the poor. When she was a teenager, she joined a convent of sisters called the Visitation nuns, even though her family did not want her to.

Then the French Revolution came. The convent was closed, and the sisters were sent away. Philippine took care of the poor and the sick, opened a school for homeless children, and bravely helped priests who were hiding.
Later, Philippine joined a new community called the Society of the Sacred Heart. Its leader, Mother Madeleine Sophie Barat, became her lifelong friend.

Ever since she was a girl, Philippine had wanted to be a missionary in America. In 1818, when she was 49, her dream came true. She and four sisters sailed for eleven weeks across the ocean to New Orleans.

The bishop sent them to St. Charles, Missouri, a tiny village on the frontier. There, in a log cabin, Philippine opened the first free school for girls west of the Mississippi River. Life was very hard. It was cold, money was scarce, and she struggled to learn English. But she kept going and opened more schools.

When she was 72, Philippine finally went to serve Native people at Sugar Creek, Kansas, where the sisters opened a school for the Potawatomi. She was too old to learn their language, so she spent many hours praying. The Potawatomi called her "Woman-Who-Prays-Always."
After about a year, she returned to St. Charles. She died there on November 18, 1852, at age 83. In 1988, Pope John Paul II declared her a saint.

pages.subtitle: A French Jesuit missionary in North America who returned to the place where he had suffered, hoping to make peace.

quick_facts.label: From
quick_facts.value: Orléans, France; served in Canada and New York

quick_facts.label: Known for
quick_facts.value: His courage and forgiveness as a missionary and martyr

pages.intro: Isaac Jogues was a Jesuit priest from France who came to North America to share the faith. He was captured and held prisoner for more than a year. After he escaped, he could have stayed safe in France. Instead, he came back to North America to work for peace. He gave his life there in 1646 and is honored as a martyr.
story_paragraphs: Isaac Jogues was born in Orléans, France, in 1607. He joined the Jesuits, a community of priests, and became a teacher. But he longed to be a missionary.

In 1636, Isaac was ordained a priest and sent to New France, which is now Canada. For six years, he lived and worked among the Huron people, also called the Wendat, near Georgian Bay. He learned about their lives and shared the Gospel with them.

At that time, the Huron and the nations of the Iroquois were at war. In 1642, Iroquois warriors captured Father Jogues, a lay helper named René Goupil, and a group of Huron Christians. They were taken to a Mohawk village. René Goupil was killed. Father Jogues was badly hurt and was kept as a prisoner for thirteen months.

With help from Dutch settlers, Father Jogues escaped and sailed home to France. His hands had been so badly injured that a priest was not normally allowed to say Mass that way. But the pope gave him special permission, saying it would be shameful to stop a martyr of Christ from offering Mass.

Father Jogues could have stayed in France. Instead, he went back to North America. In 1646, the French and the Mohawk had made peace, and he was sent to the Mohawk village of Ossernenon, in what is now New York, to help keep it.
But some Mohawk blamed the French and the missionaries for sickness and other troubles. On October 18, 1646, Father Jogues was killed. A young Frenchman named Jean de Lalande was killed the next day.
In 1930, the Church declared Isaac Jogues, René Goupil, Jean de Lalande and five other Jesuit missionaries saints. Together they are called the North American Martyrs.

pages.subtitle: The first saint born in the Americas, who worked in her garden, prayed, and cared for the sick and poor in her home.

quick_facts.label: Known for
quick_facts.value: Being the first saint born in the Americas, and caring for the poor and sick

pages.intro: Rose of Lima was born in Lima, Peru, in 1586. Her real name was Isabel, but everyone called her Rose. She loved God with her whole heart. She grew flowers and sewed to help her family, prayed in a little hut in the garden, and turned a room of her home into a place to care for the poor and sick. She was the first saint born in the Americas.
story_paragraphs: Isabel Flores de Oliva was born in Lima, Peru, on April 20, 1586. Her family called her Rosa, or Rose, and that is the name the world remembers.
From the time she was small, Rose loved to pray. She admired Saint Catherine of Siena, and she wanted to give her whole life to God, just as Catherine had.

Rose's family had money troubles. So Rose worked hard to help. During the day, she grew flowers in the garden. At night, she sewed beautiful lace and embroidery. She sold the flowers and the sewing to help her family and to give to the poor.

Her parents wanted her to marry, and they would not let her join a convent. So in 1606, Rose joined the Third Order of Saint Dominic. That meant she could follow the Dominican way of prayer while still living at home.
Rose built a small hut in her family's garden. There she spent many hours alone with God in prayer. She also made many sacrifices to grow closer to Jesus.

Rose never forgot people in need. In her last years, she set up a room in her family's house to care for homeless children, elderly people and the sick. Some people call this the beginning of social services in Peru.

Rose died on August 24, 1617, when she was only 31 years old. The whole city of Lima mourned her. In 1671, Pope Clement X declared her a saint. She was the first person born in the Americas to be named a saint. She is a patron saint of Peru, of South America, and of gardeners and florists.

pages.subtitle: A Jesuit priest in Colombia who spent 40 years caring for enslaved Africans as they arrived by ship.

quick_facts.label: From
quick_facts.value: Catalonia, Spain; served in Cartagena, Colombia

quick_facts.label: Known for
quick_facts.value: Caring for enslaved Africans and treating every person with dignity

pages.intro: Peter Claver was a Jesuit priest from Spain who served in Cartagena, Colombia. In his time, ships carried enslaved people from Africa to Cartagena. Slavery was a terrible wrong. Peter met the ships, brought food and medicine, and told the people that God loved them. He called himself "the slave of the Africans forever."
story_paragraphs: Peter Claver was born in Spain in 1580 or 1581. In 1602, he joined the Jesuits. He wanted to serve God as a missionary in the Americas.
In 1610, Peter sailed to Cartagena, a port city in what is now Colombia. He was ordained a priest there in 1616.

At that time, Cartagena was one of the biggest slave markets in the Americas. Ships brought thousands of African men, women and children who had been taken from their homes and forced across the ocean. They were treated as if they were not people at all. This was a terrible injustice, a great sin.

Another Jesuit, Father Alfonso de Sandoval, had already spent many years serving the enslaved people of Cartagena. Peter joined his work. He made a promise and called himself "the slave of the Africans forever."

Whenever a ship arrived, Peter went down into the crowded ship to care for people who were sick and weak. When they came ashore, he brought them food, fresh water, medicine and fruit. With the help of interpreters, he taught them about Jesus and reminded them that every one of them was a child of God, deeply loved.

For about 40 years, Peter cared for enslaved people. He is thought to have taught and baptized about 300,000 people. When he went to the countryside, he chose to stay in the huts of enslaved workers instead of in the owners' big houses.

In his last years, Peter was very sick and could hardly move. He died in Cartagena in September 1654. In 1888, Pope Leo XIII declared him a saint. He is the patron saint of Colombia and of people of the African diaspora.

pages.subtitle: Young Christians in Uganda who stayed faithful to Jesus, led by a brave young man who protected them.

quick_facts.label: From
quick_facts.value: Buganda, in what is now Uganda

quick_facts.label: Known for
quick_facts.value: Protecting the young pages and staying faithful to Jesus

pages.intro: Charles Lwanga was a young man who served at the court of the king of Buganda, in what is now Uganda. He helped lead the king's pages, boys and young men who worked in the royal household. When the king demanded that they do wrong and give up their faith, Charles protected them and taught them about Jesus. They gave their lives in 1886.
story_paragraphs: In 1879, Catholic missionaries called the White Fathers came to the kingdom of Buganda, in East Africa. Many people there were glad to learn about Jesus. Some of them worked at the royal court as pages, serving the king.

At first, the old king allowed Christians to live in peace. But the new king, Mwanga, began to turn against them. In 1885, Joseph Mukasa, the head of the pages and a Catholic, told the king he was doing wrong. The king had him put to death.

Charles Lwanga, Joseph's assistant, became the leader of the pages. The pages were boys and young men, from about 13 to 30 years old. The king wanted them to do things that were wrong and against God's law. Charles protected them and encouraged them to stay faithful.

On the night Joseph Mukasa died, Charles asked to be baptized. Later, when he knew the king would soon arrest the pages, Charles secretly baptized the young men who had been preparing to become Christians, so they could die as members of the Church.

The king ordered the Christian pages to give up their faith. They refused. They were marched to a place called Namugongo. On June 3, 1886, Charles Lwanga and many of his companions were put to death there. Anglican Christians were martyred with them. The youngest of the Catholic martyrs, Kizito, was only a boy.
The martyrs died praying and forgiving. Their courage did not stop the Church in Uganda. It grew stronger.
In 1964, Pope Paul VI declared 22 of the Ugandan martyrs saints. Today, a great basilica stands at Namugongo, and Christians from across Africa come there to honor them every June 3.

timeline.text: Catholic missionaries, the White Fathers, arrive in Buganda.
Joseph Mukasa, head of the pages, is put to death. Charles Lwanga is baptized.
King Mwanga orders the Christian pages arrested. Charles baptizes the young catechumens.
Charles Lwanga and many companions are put to death at Namugongo.
Pope Benedict XV declares them Blessed.
Pope Paul VI declares 22 Ugandan martyrs saints.
A basilica in their honor opens at Namugongo.

fun_facts: The 22 Ugandan martyrs were the first saints from sub-Saharan Africa.
The pages were between about 13 and 30 years old.
Anglican Christians were also martyred alongside the Catholics.
The basilica at Namugongo is round, like a traditional African hut.
Charles Lwanga is a patron saint of young people in Africa.

words_to_know.definition: A boy or young man who served in a royal household.
A person who is put to death because of their faith in Jesus.
A person preparing to be baptized.
A person sent to share the faith in another place.
Doing what is right even when you are afraid.

pages.think_about_it: Charles protected the younger pages and helped them stay faithful. How can you look out for kids who are younger than you?
pages.reflection_question: The Ugandan martyrs said no to doing wrong, even when a king commanded it. When is it hard for you to say no to something wrong?
pages.kindness_prompt: Charles Lwanga looked out for the younger pages. Look out for a younger child this week: help them, include them, or stand up for them if someone is unkind.

quiz.prompt: What job did Charles Lwanga have at the royal court?
quiz.explanation: Charles was assistant to the head of the pages and became their leader after Joseph Mukasa died.

quiz.prompt: In what country did these martyrs live?
quiz.explanation: They lived in the kingdom of Buganda, which is now part of Uganda.

quiz.prompt: What did Charles do for the young men preparing for baptism?

choices.text: He hid them in a cave

quiz.explanation: Charles secretly baptized those who were still preparing, so they could die as members of the Church.

quiz.prompt: On what date are these martyrs remembered?
quiz.explanation: Charles Lwanga and many companions gave their lives at Namugongo on June 3, 1886.

quiz.prompt: Which pope declared the 22 Ugandan martyrs saints?
quiz.explanation: Pope Paul VI declared them saints on October 18, 1964.

pages.subtitle: Twenty-six Christians in Japan, including a Japanese Jesuit and some boys, who forgave and stayed faithful to Jesus.

quick_facts.label: Known for
quick_facts.value: Forgiving his persecutors and staying faithful to Jesus

pages.intro: Paul Miki was a Japanese Jesuit and a gifted preacher. In 1597, Christians in Japan were being persecuted. Paul Miki and 25 companions, priests, brothers and lay people, including some boys, were marched to the city of Nagasaki. There they gave their lives for Jesus. Paul said he forgave the people who put them to death, just as Jesus did.
story_paragraphs: In 1549, Saint Francis Xavier brought the Gospel to Japan. Over the next years, many Japanese people became Christians.
Paul Miki was born in Japan. He became a Jesuit brother and was known as a wonderful preacher. He loved to tell people about Jesus.
But Japan's ruler, Toyotomi Hideyoshi, began to see the Christians as a danger. In 1587, he ordered the missionaries to leave. Ten years later, he ordered Christians to be arrested.

Twenty-six Christians were arrested, among them Paul Miki. Six were Franciscan friars. Three were Japanese Jesuits. Seventeen were lay people: catechists, doctors, workers, servants, old men, and some boys. They were made to walk a very long way, from the cities of Kyoto and Osaka all the way to Nagasaki.
On February 5, 1597, the twenty-six were put to death on crosses on a hill above Nagasaki, like Jesus.

Even then, Paul Miki kept preaching. He said, "I am a true Japanese." He told the crowd that he was dying because he had taught about Jesus. Then he said, "After Christ's example I forgive my persecutors." The martyrs sang and prayed as they died.

For more than 200 years after that, it was against the law to be a Christian in Japan. When missionaries came back in the 1860s, they thought no Christians were left. But they discovered that thousands of Christians near Nagasaki had kept the faith in secret, passing it on in their families. The seeds planted by the martyrs had grown.
In 1862, Pope Pius IX declared Paul Miki and his 25 companions saints.

timeline.text: Saint Francis Xavier brings the Gospel to Japan.
Japan's ruler orders the missionaries to leave.
Twenty-six Christians are arrested and made to walk to Nagasaki.
Paul Miki and 25 companions are put to death in Nagasaki.
The Church declares them Blessed.
Pope Pius IX declares them saints.
Missionaries return and find Christians who kept the faith in secret.

fun_facts: Paul Miki was a Japanese Jesuit brother and a gifted preacher.
Some of the 26 martyrs were boys.
The martyrs walked all the way from Kyoto and Osaka to Nagasaki.
Christians in Japan kept the faith in secret for more than 200 years.
A large bronze monument to the 26 martyrs stands in Nagasaki.

words_to_know.definition: When people are treated cruelly because of what they believe.
A person who is put to death because of their faith in Jesus.
Members of the Church who are not priests, brothers or sisters.
A person who teaches others about the faith.
To let go of anger and stop holding a wrong against someone.

pages.think_about_it: Paul Miki forgave the people who put him to death, just as Jesus did. Why is it so hard, and so important, to forgive?
pages.reflection_question: The hidden Christians of Japan passed on their faith in their families. How does your family help you know and love Jesus?
pages.kindness_prompt: Paul Miki forgave his persecutors. Think of someone who hurt your feelings. Pray for them today, and if you can, tell them you forgive them.

quiz.prompt: Who first brought the Gospel to Japan in 1549?
quiz.explanation: Saint Francis Xavier brought the Gospel to Japan in 1549.

quiz.prompt: How many martyrs died in Nagasaki in 1597, counting Paul Miki?
quiz.explanation: Paul Miki and 25 companions, 26 in all, gave their lives in Nagasaki in 1597.

quiz.prompt: What did Paul Miki say about the people who put him to death?

choices.text: "After Christ's example I forgive my persecutors."

quiz.explanation: Like Jesus on the cross, Paul Miki forgave the people who put him to death.

quiz.prompt: What did missionaries find when they returned to Japan in the 1860s?

choices.text: Thousands of Christians who had kept the faith in secret

quiz.explanation: For more than 200 years, Christians near Nagasaki had secretly kept the faith and passed it on in their families.

quiz.prompt: Who were the 26 martyrs?

choices.text: Priests, brothers and lay people, including some boys

quiz.explanation: The 26 included Franciscan friars, Japanese Jesuits, and lay people such as catechists, doctors, workers and boys.
